name: Yoga / Surya Namaskar for height

lead: Some height programmes and forum threads promote yoga stretches and Surya Namaskar (Sun Salutation), a flowing sequence of about twelve linked postures, as a way to stand taller. The payoff people want is a lengthened, decompressed spine and better posture.

Proponents say the stretching lengthens the spine and improves posture, a route to a small change in standing height. Published studies of Sun Salutation measure energy use (about 2.9 to 7.4 METs) and muscle activation, and none was found measuring height.

paras: People do the sequence or a stretching routine regularly, often in the morning, and combine it with other posture and height habits. Results people look for are better posture and a more upright stance over weeks of practice.
Yoga is generally an ordinary physical activity with the usual strain risks. No height-specific harms are documented.

angle.text: Yoga and Surya Namaskar are used as stretching routines to lengthen the spine and improve posture so you stand a little taller. Research on yoga covers fitness and flexibility rather than height.

lead: Yoga and Surya Namaskar (Sun Salutation) turn up in height-increase programmes and forum threads as a daily stretching routine for looking taller. Surya Namaskar is a flowing sequence of about twelve linked postures associated with devotion to the Hindu sun god Surya.[1] People who use it for height aim at posture and spinal length: standing straighter, extending the spine and reducing slouch can add visible centimetres to standing height without changing bone length.

The sequence has a short documented history. No hatha yoga text recorded it before the 19th century; it was popularised in the 1920s by the Rajah of Aundh, whose 1928 book named and described it, and then folded into the teaching of Tirumalai Krishnamacharya and his students.[1] Hatha yoga as a whole was reshaped during the 20th century into a posture-based fitness and wellbeing practice that spread worldwide after about 1975.[2]

Published research on Surya Namaskar concerns energy expenditure (roughly 2.9 to 7.4 METs depending on style) and which muscles are recruited, not height.[1] Broader yoga research covers depression, anxiety, stress measures and low back pain.[3][4][5][6] Reference works describe adult height as mostly heritable, with daily and age-related changes tied to the spinal discs and posture.[7]
infobox: India; popularised in the 1920s and after
Iyengar, Sivananda, Ashtanga (types A and B)
About 2.9 to 7.4 METs depending on style[1]

paras: Height-focused programmes present stretching poses, spinal extensions and the Sun Salutation as ways to lengthen the spine and improve alignment. The sequence is done as a flowing set that moves from standing through a backbend, a forward fold and a plank-type position and back to standing, and it is often done at the start or end of a daily stretching session. Variations differ by yoga school, including Iyengar, Sivananda and Ashtanga.[1]

In looksmaxxing forum discussion, the idea is that daily yoga stretches the spine and corrects posture, for a possible half inch to an inch of standing height, perhaps more where posture is poor, and that it could help limit height loss with age. Posters in these threads explicitly say it does not make bones grow; they describe it as making a person look taller through posture.[8] Some pair it with chin tucks.[8] Other replies in the same thread were jokes, including one about standing on toes, and one person said they sleep with a resistance band, which shows how the topic sits among other low-cost height tricks.[8]

For readers interested in appearance more broadly, posture affects how tall and open a frame reads in photographs and in person, which is why alignment work such as Tadasana (mountain pose) and chest-opening backbends are popular with people trying to look taller.

Tradition links Samarth Ramdas in the 17th century with Surya Namaskar exercises, but without defined movements, and the asana sequence was first recorded as yoga in the early 20th century.[1] Bhawanrao Shriniwasrao Pant Pratinidhi, the Rajah of Aundh, popularised and named the practice in the 1920s and published The Ten-Point Way to Health: Surya Namaskars in 1928; he said it was already a common Marathi tradition, so claims that he invented it are disputed.[1] The anthropologist Joseph Alter is cited as saying no hatha yoga text recorded it before the 19th century.[1]

Krishnamacharya taught Sun Salutation classes at the Mysore Palace and, according to the scholar Mark Singleton, drew on Indian wrestlers' exercises described in the 1896 Vyayama Dipika; his students Pattabhi Jois and B. K. S. Iyengar carried the sequence into Ashtanga and Iyengar yoga.[1] Swami Sivananda originally promoted it as a health cure through sunlight, and Vishnudevananda's 1960 Complete Illustrated Book of Yoga presented it as a fitness exercise.[1] India Post issued stamps for it in 2016.[1]

The wider tradition behind it is older. The first definition of hatha yoga is attributed to a text from about 1030, the Amrtasiddhi (11th century) is the earliest substantial hatha text, and Svatmarama compiled the influential Hathayogapradipika in the 15th century.[2] Yogis were derided by urban elites from the 17th to 19th centuries, and Swami Vivekananda separated hatha's physical exercises from spiritual raja yoga; in the 20th century Krishnamacharya, Swami Kuvalayananda and others paired asanas with gymnastics and dropped most religious content, producing the fitness-oriented practice now taught.[2]

Wikipedia describes the Iyengar version as running from Tadasana through Urdhva Hastasana, a forward fold, Downward Dog, Upward Dog and Chaturanga Dandasana, then reversing back to standing. The Sivananda version adds a lunge and high plank, and Ashtanga uses type A and type B sequences, with B adding a chair pose and a warrior pose [1]. In Sivananda practice each pose is linked to one of twelve names of Surya [1].

Several of these poses involve spinal extension (Upward Dog), forward folding with the hamstrings lengthened, and standing alignment (Tadasana), which is why height-focused programmes include them [1].

Wikipedia's article on human height reports that height varies through the day, with one study of 100 children finding an average drop of about 1.5 cm from waking to late afternoon, that exercise just before measuring tends to lower it and lying down for a long time tends to raise it.[7] Age-related shrinkage is attributed to drying of the spinal discs, soft-tissue loss and posture changes linked to degenerative disease.[7] Genetics accounts for an estimated 60 to 80 percent of height differences, and growth typically slows to zero around 15 to 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males.[7]

Posture-oriented routines such as yoga work on the soft-tissue and postural side of this picture: the aim is to stand fully upright and to keep the spine long, so that measured and perceived height sit closer to a person's maximum. This is the chain proponents describe, and standing height is also reported by Wikipedia to be about 0.7 cm lower than lying length, a reminder that height depends on how the spine is loaded.[7] Studies of yoga with height as the outcome have not been found.

A 2014 study measured activation of muscle groups during Ashtanga poses and found that beginners used the pectorals more, while instructors used the deltoids and the vastus medialis more.[1] A 2016 review of 17 studies, 10 of which measured energy cost, placed Sun Salutation from light (about 2.9 METs) to vigorous (about 7.4 METs) depending on style and whether transition jumps are used.[1] These studies did not measure height.

Grace Bullock is cited as arguing that asana practice increases body awareness, which can make exercise more beneficial and safer, and the article notes that short bouts of moderate activity count towards recommended exercise totals.[1]

Broader yoga research is substantial. A 2024 network meta-analysis of exercise for depression pooled 218 trials and reported moderate reductions in depression for yoga versus active controls (Hedges g about -0.55).[5] A 2013 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials with 619 participants found moderate evidence for short-term effects of yoga on depression versus usual care,[6] a 2018 meta-analysis of 8 trials with 319 participants reported small short-term effects on anxiety versus no treatment,[4] and a 2024 meta-analysis of 24 studies updated the depression evidence.[9] A 2017 meta-analysis examined yoga and stress-related physiological measures such as blood pressure, heart rate and cortisol,[10] and a 2023 network meta-analysis of 75 trials compared exercise types for chronic low back pain.[11] A 2024 randomized trial tested virtual yoga for chronic low back pain.[3] People who are in less back pain can stand and move more comfortably, which is one route by which a regular stretching habit could change how upright they carry themselves.

A 2012 Hacker News thread titled "How Yoga Can Wreck Your Body" drew 118 comments discussing yoga-related injuries.[12] Yoga trials generally list adverse events as a secondary outcome; the 2018 anxiety meta-analysis, for example, assessed safety alongside symptom outcomes.[4] The Sun Salutation includes weight-bearing on the hands, deep forward folds and spinal extension, so teachers commonly adapt it to the practitioner, and its energy cost rises with the faster, jumping styles.[1]

No studies found measuring height change from yoga or Surya Namaskar. Related randomized trials and meta-analyses of yoga cover other outcomes, including chronic low back pain, depression, anxiety and stress measures.[3][4][5][6][10]

lore.intro: Yoga for height appears mainly in marketing and in height-gain forum threads as a gentle, low-cost routine aimed at posture and spinal length, usually alongside other cheap tricks.[8]
